ev.chn_h_song_founding.title: The yellow robe
ev.chn_h_song_founding.text: The commander of the guards, Zhao Kuangyin, has returned to the capital as emperor: at Chenqiao his soldiers threw a yellow robe over his shoulders. The city yielded without bloodshed. The new dynasty is called Song.
ev.chn_h_song_founding.note: In 960 the general Zhao Kuangyin (Taizu) was proclaimed emperor by his troops at Chenqiao and founded the Song dynasty with its capital at Kaifeng. He soon persuaded his generals to give up their commands – Song became a state run by civil officials.
ev.chn_h_shu_conquest.title: The end of Later Shu
ev.chn_h_shu_conquest.text: Song troops have entered Chengdu; Meng Chang, ruler of Later Shu, surrendered after a short war. The treasures of the Shu court are being loaded onto boats for Kaifeng – and new taxes come with them.
ev.chn_h_shu_conquest.note: The kingdom of Later Shu in Sichuan was conquered by the Song in 965. The removal of its wealth and heavy levies bred resentment that erupted in rebellion thirty years later.
ev.chn_h_exams.title: The road through the examinations
ev.chn_h_exams.text: In the capital Emperor Taizong has passed hundreds of new jinshi in a single examination – an unheard-of number. All over the country people are saying that study is now a way up even for someone from a humble family.
ev.chn_h_exams.note: Under the Song the state examinations became the main road into office: in 977 Taizong passed hundreds of candidates. Printing and private schools made preparation more accessible, though it remained hard for the poor.
ev.chn_h_exams.ignore: That’s not for people like me
ev.chn_h_wang_xiaobo.title: “Equalise rich and poor!”
ev.chn_h_wang_xiaobo.text: The tea growers and peasants of Sichuan have risen under the slogan “Equalise rich and poor!”. Their leader Wang Xiaobo has fallen, but his successor Li Shun has taken Chengdu and proclaimed himself king.
ev.chn_h_wang_xiaobo.note: The rising of Wang Xiaobo and Li Shun (993–995) broke out over the state tea monopoly and heavy levies. Li Shun took Chengdu in 994; the revolt was crushed in 995.
ev.chn_h_wang_xiaobo.join.success: You survived the rout and came home with plunder.
ev.chn_h_wang_xiaobo.join.failure: Government troops smashed the band. You were badly wounded.
ev.chn_h_chanyuan.title: The peace of Chanyuan
ev.chn_h_chanyuan.text: News has come: peace has been made with the Khitans at Chanyuan. Every year the treasury will send silver and silk north – but there will be no more raids.
ev.chn_h_chanyuan.note: Under the Treaty of Chanyuan (1005) the Song paid the Khitan Liao empire 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year. The peace lasted more than a century.
ev.chn_h_jiaozi.title: Government jiaozi
ev.chn_h_jiaozi.text: The treasury has taken over the paper jiaozi: a bureau has opened in Chengdu that prints notes bearing seals and an expiry date. No more hauling sacks of iron coins to market.
ev.chn_h_jiaozi.note: Sichuan used heavy iron coins, so local merchants began issuing paper receipts. In 1023–1024 the state set up the Jiaozi Bureau in Chengdu – the world’s first government-issued paper money.
ev.chn_h_new_policies.title: The New Policies
ev.chn_h_new_policies.text: Chancellor Wang Anshi is bringing in the “New Policies”: state loans to farmers, cash payments instead of labour service, the baojia militia. Some call him the treasury’s saviour, others the wrecker of the old ways; Sima Guang and Su Shi oppose him.
ev.chn_h_new_policies.note: Wang Anshi’s reforms (1069–1085) aimed to fill the treasury and strengthen the army. They split officialdom into “new” and “old” factions; after Emperor Shenzong died in 1085 most were repealed, then restored again.
ev.chn_h_maritime_office.title: The maritime trade office
ev.chn_h_maritime_office.text: An Office of Maritime Trade has opened in Quanzhou. Foreign ships now come straight here instead of through Guangzhou – there is more work in the harbour and warehouses.
ev.chn_h_maritime_office.note: The Office of Maritime Trade (shibosi) was established in Quanzhou in 1087. In the twelfth to fourteenth centuries the city became one of the world’s greatest ports; Arab traders called it Zaitun.
ev.chn_h_fang_la.title: Fang La’s rebellion
ev.chn_h_fang_la.text: Fang La, a lacquer-grove owner ruined by levies for the emperor’s garden of strange rocks, has risen in revolt. His men have taken Hangzhou, are burning government offices and killing officials.
ev.chn_h_fang_la.note: Fang La’s rebellion (1120–1121) in Zhejiang was provoked by the “flowers and rocks” levies for Emperor Huizong’s garden. The rebels took Hangzhou; the revolt was crushed in spring 1121.
ev.chn_h_fang_la.stay.success: The rebels passed your lane by.
ev.chn_h_fang_la.stay.failure: They broke in, took everything of value and beat you.
ev.chn_h_jingkang.title: The fall of Kaifeng
ev.chn_h_jingkang.text: The Jurchen army besieged the capital. The city paid ransoms in gold and silk, but fell all the same: both emperors, the old and the young, were led away north into captivity with thousands of courtiers.
ev.chn_h_jingkang.note: The “Jingkang Incident”: in 1127 the Jurchen Jin took Kaifeng and carried off the emperors Huizong and Qinzong. North China passed to the Jin, and the Song court fled south – the beginning of the Southern Song.
ev.chn_h_jingkang.stay.success: You survived the sack. New banners fly over the city.
ev.chn_h_jingkang.stay.failure: You were badly hurt during the sack.
ev.chn_h_wuzhu_raid.title: The Jurchens at Hangzhou
ev.chn_h_wuzhu_raid.text: The Jurchen general Wuzhu has reached Hangzhou in pursuit of the young emperor Gaozong. The emperor has fled out to sea, and the city has been sacked and set on fire.
ev.chn_h_wuzhu_raid.note: In the winter of 1129–1130 a Jin army under Wuzhu crossed the Yangzi and took Hangzhou and Ningbo. Gaozong escaped by ship; on the way back Wuzhu was defeated by Han Shizhong.
ev.chn_h_wuzhu_raid.bury.success: The hoard survived, and so did you.
ev.chn_h_wuzhu_raid.bury.failure: The soldiers found both the cache and you.
ev.chn_h_linan.title: A temporary resting place
ev.chn_h_linan.text: The court has settled in Hangzhou for good and named it Lin’an – “Temporary Resting Place”. Temporary looks like it will last: palaces and offices are going up, and officials, merchants and craftsmen are flocking in.
ev.chn_h_linan.note: In 1138 Hangzhou (Lin’an) became the de facto capital of the Southern Song. By the thirteenth century it had, by various estimates, around a million inhabitants.
ev.chn_h_yue_fei.title: Yue Fei
ev.chn_h_yue_fei.text: General Yue Fei, who had beaten the Jurchens again and again, has been put to death in prison. They say Chancellor Qin Hui slandered him for the sake of peace with the Jin. The city whispers, but no one speaks aloud.
ev.chn_h_yue_fei.note: Yue Fei was executed in early 1142 (the end of the 11th year of Shaoxing) on a charge now held to be false. Under the Shaoxing peace the Song accepted vassal status and paid tribute to the Jin. Yue Fei was later rehabilitated and revered as a model of loyalty.
ev.chn_h_kaifeng_siege.title: Siege and plague
ev.chn_h_kaifeng_siege.text: The Mongols are besieging Kaifeng, the last capital of the Jin. In the refugee-crowded city an epidemic has broken out – people die faster than they can be buried.
ev.chn_h_kaifeng_siege.note: In 1232 the Mongols besieged Kaifeng. An epidemic broke out during the siege; contemporaries wrote of hundreds of thousands dead in fifty days – a figure probably exaggerated. The city surrendered in 1233.
ev.chn_h_kaifeng_siege.care.failure: You caught it and hovered between life and death for a long time.
ev.chn_h_kaifeng_siege.isolate.success: You waited out the disaster behind a barred gate.
ev.chn_h_kaifeng_siege.isolate.failure: The sickness found you all the same.
ev.chn_h_chengdu_1236.title: The Mongols in Sichuan
ev.chn_h_chengdu_1236.text: A Mongol army has stormed into Chengdu. The city that has survived so many wars is all but destroyed; the survivors are fleeing into the mountains.
ev.chn_h_chengdu_1236.note: In 1236 Mongol forces under Köten took and sacked Chengdu. War in Sichuan dragged on for nearly half a century and devastated the province.
ev.chn_h_chengdu_1236.hide.success: You crawled out of the cellar three days later into a ruined city.
ev.chn_h_chengdu_1236.hide.failure: The soldiers found the hiding place.
ev.chn_h_xiangyang.title: The war levy
ev.chn_h_xiangyang.text: The Mongols are in the fifth year of their siege of Xiangyang, the key to the Yangzi. The treasury needs soldiers and money; in the counties men are seized right off the roads.
ev.chn_h_xiangyang.note: The siege of Xiangyang and Fancheng (1268–1273) sealed the fate of the Southern Song. The cities fell after Muslim engineers built heavy counterweight trebuchets for the Mongols.
ev.chn_h_xiangyang.serve.success: You came back alive, though you saw things no one talks about.
ev.chn_h_xiangyang.serve.failure: You were badly wounded in battle.
ev.chn_h_xiangyang.hide.failure: You were found and fined, and the neighbours look askance.
ev.chn_h_linan_surrender.title: Lin’an surrenders
ev.chn_h_linan_surrender.text: The Mongol general Bayan stands at the gates of the capital. The empress dowager has sent him the imperial seal – Lin’an has surrendered without a fight, and the city is almost untouched. Song loyalists are heading south to the sea.
ev.chn_h_linan_surrender.note: In early 1276 Lin’an surrendered to the Mongols, and the child emperor was taken north. Song loyalists fought on in the south until their fleet was destroyed at Yamen in 1279.
ev.chn_h_linan_surrender.accept: Go on living under the new rulers
ev.chn_h_linan_surrender.loyal: Go south with the Song loyalists
ev.chn_h_pu_shougeng.title: The gates are shut
ev.chn_h_pu_shougeng.text: Pu Shougeng, superintendent of maritime trade and scion of an Arab merchant family, has gone over to the Mongols and shut the gates against the fleeing Song court. Members of the Song imperial clan in the city have been massacred.
ev.chn_h_pu_shougeng.note: Pu Shougeng, who had long controlled Quanzhou’s maritime trade, handed the city to the Yuan in 1276–1277. Under the Yuan he and his family kept enormous influence.
ev.chn_h_dadu.title: The Great Capital
ev.chn_h_dadu.text: Khubilai is completing his new capital, Dadu: straight broad streets, rammed-earth walls, lakes in the heart of the city. Tens of thousands of labourers toil on the works, and people from all over the empire are moving in.
ev.chn_h_dadu.note: Construction of Dadu (Khanbaliq in Turkic) began in 1267; from 1272 it was the capital of the Yuan empire, and building went on into the mid-1280s. Its plan became the basis of later Beijing.
ev.chn_h_four_classes.title: The four ranks
ev.chn_h_four_classes.text: Under the Mongols people are sorted into ranks: Mongols, “coloured-eyed” westerners, Han from the north, and “southerners”, the former Song subjects. The high posts go to the first; southerners get whatever is left.
ev.chn_h_four_classes.text.beijing: Under the Mongols people are sorted into ranks: Mongols, “coloured-eyed” westerners, northern Han and “southerners”. In the capital you see it at once: Mongols and semuren sit in the offices, with Han as their clerks.
ev.chn_h_four_classes.note: The Yuan division into Mongols, semuren, Hanren and Nanren shaped quotas for office and examinations. Historians debate how far it was a formal system and how far just practice.
ev.chn_h_marco_polo.title: A man from the land of the Franks
ev.chn_h_marco_polo.text: They say a merchant from the distant land of the Franks serves the khan. He has travelled half the world and asks about everything: the bridges, the paper money, the black stones that burn in stoves.
ev.chn_h_marco_polo.note: The Venetian Marco Polo claimed to have served Khubilai in 1275–1292 and to have visited Hangzhou and Quanzhou. Most historians accept his account in substance, but the debate continues: his name does not appear in Chinese sources.
ev.chn_h_epidemics.title: Pestilence
ev.chn_h_epidemics.text: Pestilence is sweeping the land: villages die out, and there is no one to bury the dead on the roads. Some blame floods and famine; others the wrath of Heaven against the Mongol rulers.
ev.chn_h_epidemics.note: Yuan annals record many epidemics in the 1330s–1350s. Whether they were linked to the Black Death then ravaging Europe and the Middle East is debated.
ev.chn_h_epidemics.care.failure: You caught it and hovered between life and death for a long time.
ev.chn_h_epidemics.isolate.success: You waited out the disaster behind a barred gate.
ev.chn_h_epidemics.isolate.failure: The sickness found you all the same.
ev.chn_h_red_turbans.title: The Red Turbans
ev.chn_h_red_turbans.text: A hundred and fifty thousand men were driven to mend the Yellow River dikes, paper money is worthless – and it all caught fire. The Red Turbans have risen to the cry: “Maitreya has come, the Prince of Light is born!”
ev.chn_h_red_turbans.note: The Red Turban rebellion began in 1351, when huge numbers of labourers were conscripted to re-dig the Yellow River’s channel. It was led by White Lotus followers; the founder of the Ming, Zhu Yuanzhang, rose from this movement.
ev.chn_h_red_turbans.join.success: You marched across half the country with your band and came home with plunder and renown.
ev.chn_h_red_turbans.join.failure: Yuan troops smashed your band. You were badly wounded.
ev.chn_h_ispah.title: The Ispah rebellion
ev.chn_h_ispah.text: Quanzhou’s Persian garrison – the Ispah – has mutinied. For years the city changes hands, and after the rebels’ defeat the mob takes revenge on all foreign merchants alike.
ev.chn_h_ispah.note: The Ispah rebellion (1357–1366) began among Persian Muslim mercenaries and ended in a massacre of the Muslim community, including the Pu family. Quanzhou’s overseas trade declined afterwards.
ev.chn_h_ispah.shelter.success: Your neighbour survived. Such things are not forgotten.
ev.chn_h_ispah.shelter.failure: The mob broke into your house too.
ev.chn_h_ming_founding.title: The Bright Dynasty
ev.chn_h_ming_founding.text: Zhu Yuanzhang, once a beggar monk and rebel leader, has proclaimed a new dynasty in Nanjing – the Ming, the “Bright”. The Mongol emperor is fleeing to the steppe.
ev.chn_h_ming_founding.note: In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang (reign name Hongwu) founded the Ming dynasty with its capital at Nanjing. That summer his armies took Dadu.
ev.chn_h_dadu_falls.title: The khan flees
ev.chn_h_dadu_falls.text: The Ming general Xu Da has reached Dadu. Emperor Toghon Temür fled with his court through the northern gate by night, and the city surrendered almost without a fight. Dadu is now called Beiping – “the North Pacified”.
ev.chn_h_dadu_falls.note: In September 1368 Xu Da’s troops occupied Dadu; the last Yuan emperor fled to Mongolia. The city was renamed Beiping and lost its status as capital – until 1421.
ev.chn_h_dadu_falls.welcome: Go out to greet the Ming troops
ev.chn_h_xia_falls.title: The end of the Xia kingdom
ev.chn_h_xia_falls.text: Ming troops have entered Chengdu. The Xia kingdom, founded here by the Red Turban leader Ming Yuzhen, has fallen: his young heir has surrendered.
ev.chn_h_xia_falls.note: Ming Yuzhen founded the Xia state in Sichuan in 1362–1363. After his death in 1366 the throne passed to the boy Ming Sheng, who surrendered to the Ming in 1371.
ev.chn_h_haijin.title: Not a plank on the sea
ev.chn_h_haijin.text: The emperor has forbidden private ships to put to sea: “not a single plank on the sea”. The maritime trade office is closed; overseas trade is now allowed only through tribute embassies.
ev.chn_h_haijin.note: From 1371 the Hongwu emperor imposed the sea ban (haijin); in 1374 the Quanzhou maritime trade office was closed. The ban, with interruptions, lasted until 1567 and bred massive smuggling.
ev.chn_h_haijin.smuggle.success: Night boats run out to the islands, and the silver keeps coming.
ev.chn_h_haijin.smuggle.failure: The coast guard intercepted the boat.
ev.chn_h_purges.title: The Hu Weiyong case
ev.chn_h_purges.text: Chancellor Hu Weiyong has been executed for conspiracy, and arrests are spreading across the country: anyone with the slightest tie to him is seized – kin, friends, anyone who once wrote him a letter.
ev.chn_h_purges.note: In 1380 the Hongwu emperor executed Chancellor Hu Weiyong and abolished the office of chancellor. The “Hu case” dragged on for years and, by traditional accounts, cost some thirty thousand lives.
ev.chn_h_purges.burn.success: The ashes were scattered in the garden. No one came for you.
ev.chn_h_purges.burn.failure: A letter turned up in someone else’s house.
ev.chn_h_purges.lie_low: Lie low and see no one
ev.chn_h_zheng_he.title: The treasure fleet
ev.chn_h_zheng_he.text: The eunuch Zheng He is assembling a vast fleet: dozens of “treasure ships” and nearly thirty thousand men will sail for the Western Ocean – to Java, Ceylon, Calicut. Sailors, carpenters and interpreters are being hired.
ev.chn_h_zheng_he.note: Zheng He’s seven voyages (1405–1433) reached India, Arabia and East Africa. The first carried some 27,800 men. After 1433 the voyages were stopped.
ev.chn_h_zheng_he.sign.success: You saw the giraffe being brought to the emperor, and came home with your pay and stories for a lifetime.
ev.chn_h_zheng_he.sign.failure: A storm off Java. You came home barely alive.
ev.chn_h_forbidden_city.title: The Forbidden City
ev.chn_h_forbidden_city.text: The Yongle emperor is building a new palace in Beijing. Logs are floated from the forests of Sichuan, stone is dragged over the ice from the quarries, and workers are being gathered from across the country.
ev.chn_h_forbidden_city.note: The Forbidden City was built from 1406 to 1420 by, it is estimated, hundreds of thousands of workers. In 1421 Beijing officially became the Ming capital.
ev.chn_h_forbidden_city.avoid.failure: They found you anyway and fined you.
ev.chn_h_tumu.title: Disaster at Tumu
ev.chn_h_tumu.text: Terrible news: the emperor, led on campaign against the Oirats by the eunuch Wang Zhen, has been defeated at Tumu fortress and taken prisoner. The Oirats are marching on Beijing. Minister Yu Qian is calling everyone to the walls.
ev.chn_h_tumu.note: In 1449 the Ming army was crushed by Esen’s Oirats at Tumu, and the Zhengtong emperor was captured. Yu Qian enthroned the emperor’s brother and successfully defended Beijing; Esen withdrew.
ev.chn_h_tumu.defend.success: The Oirats fell back from the walls. The whole street sings your praises.
ev.chn_h_tumu.defend.failure: An arrow found you at the battlements.
ev.chn_h_altan.title: Fire beyond the walls
ev.chn_h_altan.text: The Mongol Altan Khan has broken through the Wall and is burning the outskirts of Beijing. The gates are shut, the troops won’t come out, and all night the glow of fires is visible beyond the walls.
ev.chn_h_altan.note: In 1550 (the gengxu year) Altan Khan reached Beijing and plundered its surroundings for days, seeking the right to trade with China. He obtained trading rights in 1571.
ev.chn_h_wokou.title: Pirates on the coast
ev.chn_h_wokou.text: The wokou pirates are burning coastal towns again. General Qi Jiguang is recruiting a militia of peasants and miners and drilling them to fight in the “mandarin duck” formation.
ev.chn_h_wokou.note: In the 1550s–1560s wokou raids ravaged the coasts of Zhejiang and Fujian. Most of the pirates were Chinese smugglers. Qi Jiguang and Yu Dayou crushed them by the mid-1560s; in 1567 the sea ban was relaxed.
ev.chn_h_wokou.militia.success: Qi Jiguang’s band routed the pirates. You came home with a reward.
ev.chn_h_wokou.militia.failure: You were wounded in a skirmish on the shore.
ev.chn_h_wokou.hide: Take your goods to the hills
ev.chn_h_great_wall.title: The brick wall
ev.chn_h_great_wall.text: On the mountains to the north a wall of brick is going up – with towers where garrisons live all year round. General Qi Jiguang is hiring masons and soldiers.
ev.chn_h_great_wall.note: Most of the Great Wall that survives today was built under the Ming in the sixteenth century. From 1568 Qi Jiguang, commanding the defences north of Beijing, built some 1,200 brick watchtowers.
ev.chn_h_single_whip.title: The Single Whip
ev.chn_h_single_whip.text: Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng has introduced the “Single Whip” across the empire: taxes and labour duties are rolled into one payment in silver. The silver comes from overseas – from the Japanese and from the bearded westerners in Manila.
ev.chn_h_single_whip.note: The Single Whip reform was extended to the whole empire in 1581. China’s vast demand for silver drew in Japanese mines and Spanish American silver shipped via Manila (founded 1571).
ev.chn_h_mining_eunuchs.title: The tax eunuchs
ev.chn_h_mining_eunuchs.text: The Wanli emperor has sent eunuchs out to collect mining taxes and trade duties. They take from whom they like, as much as they like; in Suzhou, they say, the weavers have already beaten up the collectors.
ev.chn_h_mining_eunuchs.note: From 1596 the Wanli emperor sent eunuch commissioners to collect mining and commercial taxes in the provinces. In Fujian the eunuch Gao Cai ran riot; in 1601 the weavers of Suzhou rose against the collector Sun Long.
ev.chn_h_mining_eunuchs.riot: Take to the streets with your neighbours
ev.chn_h_mining_eunuchs.riot.success: The collector fled the city. His office was burned.
ev.chn_h_mining_eunuchs.riot.failure: The guards seized the ringleaders – and you among them.
ev.chn_h_late_famine.title: The years of calamity
ev.chn_h_late_famine.text: Drought, locusts and famine sweep the land year after year. Rice costs ten times what it did, the roads are crowded with refugees, and in the villages people eat bark.
ev.chn_h_late_famine.note: In the late 1630s and early 1640s China suffered a series of droughts and crop failures that coincided with the cooling of the “Little Ice Age”. The famine fuelled the rebellions of Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong.
ev.chn_h_late_famine.hoard: Keep the stores for your own
ev.chn_h_beijing_plague.title: Plague in the capital
ev.chn_h_beijing_plague.text: Plague in Beijing: people die so fast that there are not enough coffins. The soldiers on the walls are sick too – there is no one to stand guard.
ev.chn_h_beijing_plague.note: In 1641–1644 an epidemic (probably plague) raged in north China. In 1643 a huge share of Beijing’s population died, weakening the city’s defence against the rebels.
ev.chn_h_beijing_plague.care.failure: You caught it and hovered between life and death for a long time.
ev.chn_h_beijing_plague.isolate.success: You waited out the disaster behind a barred gate.
ev.chn_h_beijing_plague.isolate.failure: The sickness found you all the same.
ev.chn_h_li_zicheng.title: The end of the Ming
ev.chn_h_li_zicheng.text: Li Zicheng’s army has entered Beijing. The Chongzhen emperor hanged himself from a tree on Coal Hill behind the palace. The Ming dynasty has fallen – and the Manchus, they say, are already coming from the north.
ev.chn_h_li_zicheng.note: On 25 April 1644 Li Zicheng’s rebels took Beijing and the Chongzhen emperor took his own life. Six weeks later General Wu Sangui let the Manchus through the Shanhai Pass, and the Qing dynasty took the throne in Beijing.
ev.chn_h_li_zicheng.welcome: Open the gate and pay them off
ev.chn_h_li_zicheng.hide.success: The rebels took a little and moved on.
ev.chn_h_li_zicheng.hide.failure: The rebels beat silver out of every household – including yours.
ev.chn_h_zhang_xianzhong.title: The Great Western Kingdom
ev.chn_h_zhang_xianzhong.text: The rebel Zhang Xianzhong has taken Chengdu and proclaimed his own Great Western Kingdom. Such stories are told of his cruelty that whole villages are fleeing to the mountains.
ev.chn_h_zhang_xianzhong.note: In 1644 Zhang Xianzhong took Chengdu and founded the Great Western Kingdom (Daxi). His rule was marked by mass killings; their scale is disputed, but Sichuan’s population fell drastically.
ev.chn_h_zhang_xianzhong.stay.success: You survived, giving up almost everything.
